stem: Two machines produce bolts. Machine X: mean diameter 12 mm, standard deviation 0.6 mm. Machine Y: mean diameter 20 mm, standard deviation 0.8 mm. A quality engineer wants to know which machine produces bolts with MORE uniform relative consistency. Which machine has lower CV and by how much?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Student compares absolute SDs (0.6 vs 0.8) and incorrectly concludes X is more consistent because 0.6 < 0.8, ignoring that means differ. CV_X = 5%, CV_Y = 4%, so Y is more consistent.
CV_X = (0.6/12) x 100 = 5%. CV_Y = (0.8/20) x 100 = 4%. Machine Y has lower CV (4% vs 5%), so Y is more uniformly consistent. Difference = 5% - 4% = 1%.

Student correctly identifies X as higher CV but miscalculates the difference as 2% instead of 1%, or computes CV_X = 5% and CV_Y = 3% (dividing 0.8/20 as 0.04 then shifting decimal, yielding 4% but rounding to 3%), giving a difference of 2%.
Student computes CV_Y = (0.8/20) x 100 = 4% correctly but misreads CV_X = 0.6/12 x 100 as 6% (decimal slip), giving difference = 6% - 4% = 2%, and still picks Y.

explanation: CV_X = (0.6/12) x 100 = 5%. CV_Y = (0.8/20) x 100 = 4%. Machine Y has the lower CV, making it more consistent in relative terms. The difference is 5% - 4% = 1%. Comparing absolute SDs (0.6 vs 0.8) is misleading because the machines produce bolts of different sizes.

explanation_sections.punchline: When mean sizes differ, only CV reveals which is more consistent - not the absolute SD.
explanation_sections.approach: Formula selection: use CV = (SD/mean) x 100 for comparing consistency across groups with different means. Compute CV_X = (0.6/12) x 100 = 5%; CV_Y = (0.8/20) x 100 = 4%. Lower CV = more consistent. Difference = 1 percentage point.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always use CV when comparing variability of measurements with different magnitudes or units.
explanation_sections.timing: About 60 seconds. Trap: comparing SDs directly (0.6 < 0.8) leads to picking X, which is wrong. Always compute CV when means differ.
